hints: Count the total outer shell electrons first. H brings 1, C brings 4, N brings 5 and O brings 6, so think how many dots and crosses must appear in total.
Keep the atoms in the order written, H-O-C-N and H-N-C-O, and join them with single or multiple bonds so that C, N and O each end up with a full octet.
Check where the triple bond must go and where the lone pairs sit to satisfy all octets while keeping H with only 2 electrons.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons you must show**
You have one H (1) + one C (4) + one N (5) + one O (6) = 16 outer electrons in each molecule. That is your check total. H can only hold 2 electrons in a single bond, while C, N and O want 8 each.

Build HOCN, cyanic acid**
Line them up H-O-C-N. H-O is single, O-C is single. That leaves C and N short of octets. Put a triple bond between C and N, $\text{H-O-C}\equiv\text{N}$. Now give O two lone pairs and N one lone pair. Count again and you have 16.

Build HNCO, isocyanic acid**
Line them up H-N-C-O. H-N is single. To complete octets here you need two double bonds, $\text{H-N=C=O}$. Give N one lone pair and O two lone pairs. Again the total is 16 electrons and every atom except H has an octet.
Final answer: H-O-C≡N with H-O single, O-C single, C≡N triple; H-N=C=O with H-N single, N=C double, C=O double. Each diagram shows 16 outer shell electrons with correct lone pairs to complete octets.

hints: Look at the central atoms in H-N=C=O and count bonding pairs plus lone pairs on N and on C to predict their shapes.
walkthrough:
Read the shape from electron pairs**
In $\text{H-N=C=O}$, N has two bonding pairs plus one lone pair, so it is bent like ammonia, about $120^{\circ}$, accepted 115 to $125^{\circ}$. C has two double bond regions and no lone pair, so it is linear, $180^{\circ}$ for NCO.
Final answer: HNC = 115 to 125 degrees, NCO = 180 degrees.

hints: Compare the C-N linkage in your two diagrams, one is C triple N and the other is C double N, then recall how bond order affects length.
walkthrough:
Link bond order to length**
More shared pairs pull the nuclei closer. HOCN has $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ with three shared pairs, HNCO has $\text{C=N}$ with two shared pairs. So the triple bond in cyanic acid is shorter and stronger.
Final answer: Cyanic acid, HOCN, has the shorter C-N bond because it contains a $\mathrm{C\equiv N}$ triple bond compared to a $\mathrm{C=N}$ double bond in isocyanic acid.

hints: Write $K_a = [\mathrm{H}^+][\mathrm{NCO}^-]/[\mathrm{HNCO}]$ and use the weak acid approximation that $[\mathrm{H}^+] \approx [\mathrm{NCO}^-]$ with equilibrium $[\mathrm{HNCO}] \approx 0.10$.
Recall the shortcut $[\mathrm{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c}$ and then $\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H}^+]$, watching the power of 10.
walkthrough:
Set up the weak acid calculation**
For $\text{HNCO} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{NCO}^-$, $$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{NCO}^-]}{[\text{HNCO}]}$$ Because dissociation is tiny, $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{NCO}^-]$ and $[\text{HNCO}]$ stays $0.10$. So $$[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c} = \sqrt{1.2 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.10}$$

Evaluate pH**
That gives $[\text{H}^+] = 3.46 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. Then $$\text{pH} = -\log(3.46 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.46$$ about 2.5 to one decimal place.

Final answer: $[\mathrm{H}^+] = \sqrt{0.10 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-4}} = 3.46 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$\mathrm{pH} = 2.46$

hints: List all reactants $(\mathrm{NH}_2)_2\mathrm{CO}$ and $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ and all products $\mathrm{NaNCO}$, $\mathrm{CO}_2$, $\mathrm{NH}_3$, $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$, then balance Na and N first.
walkthrough:
Balance by inspection**
You need 2 Na in $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to make 2 $\text{NaNCO}$, so put 2 in front of urea and $\text{NaNCO}$. That fixes N. Then C, H and O fall into place with one $\text{CO}_2$, two $\text{NH}_3$ and one $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2(\text{NH}_2)_2\text{CO} \rightarrow 2\text{NaNCO} + \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Final answer: $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + 2(NH_2)_2CO \rightarrow 2NaNCO + CO_2 + 2NH_3 + H_2O}$

hints: Calculate initial moles of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ remembering $\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2$ gives two $\mathrm{OH}^-$ per formula, and moles of acid neutralised from $20.0 \text{ cm}^3$ of $0.100 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ HNCO.
Subtract to find excess $\mathrm{OH}^-$ moles and divide by the new total volume $50.0 \text{ cm}^3$ in $\text{dm}^3$ to get concentration.
walkthrough:
Find moles of hydroxide added and used**
Moles $\text{Ba(OH)}_2 = 0.0300 \times 0.100 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol, so $$n(\text{OH}^-)_{initial} = 2 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-3} = 6.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ Moles acid = $0.0200 \times 0.100 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol, which consumes $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $\text{OH}^-$.

Convert excess to concentration**
Excess $n(\text{OH}^-) = (6.0-2.0) \times 10^{-3} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. Total volume = $30.0+20.0 = 50.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.0500 \text{ dm}^3$. So $$[\text{OH}^-] = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.0500} = 0.080 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
Final answer: Excess $n(\mathrm{OH}^-) = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol in $50.0 \text{ cm}^3$; $[\mathrm{OH}^-] = 0.080 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

hints: Use $K_w = [\mathrm{H}^+][\mathrm{OH}^-] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ to find $[\mathrm{H}^+]$ from your $[\mathrm{OH}^-] = 0.08$.
Apply $\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H}^+]$ and expect a strongly alkaline value above 12.
walkthrough:
Go through Kw**
$$[\text{H}^+] = \frac{K_w}{[\text{OH}^-]} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{0.080} = 1.25 \times 10^{-13} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Convert to pH**
$$\text{pH} = -\log(1.25 \times 10^{-13}) = 12.90$$ about 12.9. This makes sense because excess strong base dominates.
Final answer: $[\mathrm{H}^+] = 1.25 \times 10^{-13} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$; $\mathrm{pH} = 12.9$.

hints: Recall the starting pH is the weak acid pH from (b)(i), about 2.5, not 1.
Work out the equivalence volume where moles $\mathrm{OH}^-$ equals moles acid, remembering $\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2$ is dibasic.
Remember the final pH at $30.0 \text{ cm}^3$ is the value from (c)(ii), about 12.9, and the curve rises steeply through the end point.
walkthrough:
Anchor the start**
Plot the first point at volume 0, pH 2.46 from the weak acid calculation. It is well above 1 because HNCO is weak.

Locate the end point**
Moles acid = $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol needs $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $\text{OH}^-$, which comes from $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$. At $0.100 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ that is $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$. Draw the steep vertical jump there.

Anchor the finish**
After excess base the curve levels near 13. At $30.0 \text{ cm}^3$ the pH must be 12.9. So sketch a typical weak acid with strong base shape joining these three key points.
Final answer: Curve starts at pH 2.5, rises gradually then steeply with vertical section at $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ $\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2$ added, then flattens to finish at pH 12.9 at $30.0 \text{ cm}^3$.

hints: Think what denta means in terms of number of bonds to the metal, so monodentate means how many donor atoms per ligand.
Recall the general definition of any ligand in terms of lone pair donation to a metal ion.
walkthrough:
Define monodentate**
Mono means one. A monodentate species uses one donor atom to form one dative bond to the metal centre.

Define ligand**
A ligand is any molecule or ion with a lone pair that it donates into an empty orbital on a metal atom or ion to make a coordinate bond.

Final answer: Monodentate: forms one coordinate (dative covalent) bond to the metal.
Ligand: species that donates a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate bond to a metal atom or ion.

hints: Silver(I) in a linear complex has coordination number 2, so think how many $\mathrm{NCO}^-$ ions bind to one $\mathrm{Ag}^+$.
Add the charges, $+1$ from Ag plus two times $-1$ from cyanate, to work out the charge on the whole complex ion.
walkthrough:
Build the coordination sphere**
Linear for $\text{Ag}^+$ means two ligands. Each $\text{NCO}^-$ is monodentate, so two of them give $[\text{Ag(NCO)}_2]$.

Work out the charge**
$+1 + 2(-1) = -1$. So the formula including charge is $[\text{Ag(NCO)}_2]^-$. Bonding through N or O is both accepted.
Final answer: $[\mathrm{Ag(NCO)_2}]^-$ (or $[\mathrm{Ag(OCN)_2}]^-$).

hints: Use $n = m/M_r$ with $M_r(\mathrm{BaCO}_3) = 197.3$ and mass $1.66 \text{ g}$.
walkthrough:
Convert precipitate mass to moles**
$$n = \frac{m}{M_r} = \frac{1.66}{197.3} = 8.41 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
Final answer: $n(\mathrm{BaCO_3}) = 1.66/197.3 = 8.41 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

hints: Follow the two equations, one mole RNCO gives one mole $\mathrm{CO}_2$ which gives one mole $\mathrm{BaCO}_3$, then use $M_r = m/n$ with $1.00 \text{ g}$.
walkthrough:
Link back to the isocyanate**
$\text{RNCO} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3$ is 1:1:1, so $n(\text{RNCO}) = 8.41 \times 10^{-3}$ mol. Then $$M_r = \frac{1.00}{8.41 \times 10^{-3}} = 119$$
Final answer: $M_r(\mathrm{RNCO}) = 119$.

hints: Subtract the mass of the NCO group ($14+12+16=42$) from $119$ to leave the mass of R, then fit C and H only.
walkthrough:
Find R then the whole formula**
Mass of NCO = $14+12+16 = 42$. So mass of R = $119-42 = 77$. With C and H only, 77 fits $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ ($72+5$). Add NCO back: $\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{NO}$.
Final answer: Molecular formula $\mathrm{C_7H_5NO}$.

hints: Since R is $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5$, the amine $\mathrm{RNH}_2$ is this group attached to $\mathrm{NH}_2$, think which common aromatic amine this is.
walkthrough:
Draw the amine**
R is phenyl, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$. So $\text{RNH}_2$ is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, phenylamine. Sketch a benzene ring with an $\text{NH}_2$ group attached directly to it.
Final answer: Phenylamine, $\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}$: benzene ring with $\mathrm{NH_2}$ substituent.
